title: History often hinges on boring technical questions
gist: In a wide-ranging mailbag, Yglesias argues that quiet monetary-policy decisions — from Grant's 1874 veto to Weimar Germany's Depression response to Janet Yellen's 2016 Fed tightening — have repeatedly reshaped major political outcomes including Reconstruction's collapse, Hitler's rise, and Trump's 2016 win, while also covering Democrats' missing 2026 agenda, Silicon Valley's crank macro views, the Afghanistan withdrawal narrative, party factionalism, and vacation-town YIMBYism.

insights.claim: Despite Democrats now having a broadly reasonable slate of 2026 primary winners, the party still has no semblance of a national policy agenda — no shared set of policies candidates are actually running on.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A party can win individual races without a unifying platform, but that leaves no mandate to govern on if it takes the majority.
insights.quote: what Democrats do not have is any semblance of a national agenda — no set of policies that they are running on.
insights.locator: Strikingly, though, what Democrats do not have

insights.claim: Yglesias points to six specific policy items from the moderate manifesto 'Deciding to Win' — banning congressional stock trading, expanding Medicare to cover dental/vision/hearing, raising the minimum wage to $12, cracking down on tax evasion, spending on lead pollution reduction, and guaranteeing abortion rights nationally before 12 weeks — each of which tested with double-digit net-favorable margins in a fair poll that included partisan framing and counterarguments.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete, poll-tested menu of items that could serve as a shared platform bridging moderates and further-left Democrats.
insights.locator: I pulled these six items from section 5.5

insights.claim: Yglesias suggests swapping the lead-pollution item for a more explicitly affordability-focused message like ending the Trump tariffs, and imagines figures from Mary Peltola to Abdul El-Sayed rallying around the same six-item agenda while disagreeing on other things.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Offers a coalition-building template that could unite the party's moderate and left wings around a shared, affordability-forward message.
insights.quote: Maybe cut the lead thing and find something more explicitly affordability-focused like “end the Trump tariffs.”
insights.locator: What I like about this agenda

themes.theme: Monetary policy and the collapse of Reconstruction

insights.claim: There is deep technical disagreement over whether Ulysses S. Grant's 1874 veto of the Inflation Bill mattered: Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz's 'A Monetary History of the United States, 1867-1960' downplays the bill's significance, instead blaming the 1873 decision to stop backing currency with silver and bank reserve requirements.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Shows that even a landmark economic history disputes which specific 1870s policy lever actually drove the deflationary spiral, complicating any confident counterfactual.
insights.locator: Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz

insights.claim: Economist Charles Calomiris's 1992 article on greenbacks disputes Friedman and Schwartz, arguing the 1874 Inflation Bill would in fact have been effective in halting the deflationary spiral and reviving the economy.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Presents a live scholarly counter-view that raises the stakes of Grant's veto, since it implies the missed policy could have materially changed the economy's trajectory.
insights.quote: Charles Calomiris’s 1992 article on greenbacks says that Friedman and Schwartz are wrong and the Inflation Bill would in fact have been efficacious in halting the deflationary spiral and reviving the economy.
insights.locator: That said, Charles Calomiris’s 1992 article

insights.claim: Yglesias's counterfactual: had Grant pursued a more successful monetary policy (via either the Inflation Bill or the earlier Coinage Act), Democrats would have made smaller gains in the 1874 midterms and Rutherford B. Hayes would have carried New York and Indiana outright in 1876, avoiding the disputed election entirely.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Traces a direct causal line from a 19th-century monetary policy choice to the contested 1876 election and the subsequent bargain that ended Reconstruction.
insights.quote: Rutherford B. Hayes would have carried New York and Indiana in 1876 so the whole disputed election scenario would have been avoided.
insights.locator: If you imagine the Grant administration

insights.claim: Yglesias argues that even a stronger Hayes administration likely could not have single-handedly saved Reconstruction, since ensuring Black voting rights was not a winning issue for Republicans with Northern whites, though four more years of federal backing would have mattered for coalitions like Virginia's Readjuster Party and North Carolina's fusionist Republican-Populist alliance.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Tempers the counterfactual with realism: better monetary policy might have bought time for specific biracial political coalitions rather than permanently securing Reconstruction outright.
insights.locator: It strains credulity to argue

insights.claim: Yglesias argues the 1876 compromise that ended Reconstruction cast a retrospective air of pure opportunism over Republican support for Black voting rights, when in fact voting rights were also a genuine, profound moral issue and not solely a self-interested electoral tactic.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Pushes back on a cynical historical narrative, arguing the compromise's political convenience shouldn't erase the genuine moral stakes of the underlying rights fight.
insights.quote: in retrospect, I think we also see voting rights as genuinely one of the most profound moral issues of American history.
insights.locator: I don’t want to deny that some opportunism was in play

themes.theme: Monetary policy as an underrated force in 20th-century politics

insights.claim: Yglesias's central thesis: monetary policy is uniquely consequential for short-term prosperity and thus election outcomes, even though it's the kind of boring, technical subject ordinary voters have no strong opinions on — making it the single most underrated force in politics.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A framework for reading political upheavals (from Weimar to 2016) primarily through the lens of macroeconomic mismanagement rather than purely ideological narratives.
insights.quote: the single most underrated thing in politics is getting the technical aspects of macroeconomic policy right.
insights.locator: The moral of the story

insights.claim: In 1928, with Germany's economy hit by neither inflation nor depression, the Nazi Party finished ninth with just 2.6 percent of the vote while the Communists took fourth with 10.6 percent; by 1930, as the Depression deepened, the Nazis had risen to second place and the Communists to third.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Concrete vote-share numbers showing Nazi support was negligible absent an active economic crisis, directly tying extremist gains to the Depression's severity rather than purely ideological appeal.
insights.quote: In 1928, with the economy ravaged neither by inflation nor by depression, the Nazi Party finished in ninth place with 2.6 percent of the vote.
insights.locator: In 1928, with the economy ravaged

insights.claim: Yglesias argues that if Germany's Brüning cabinet had mounted a more effective monetary response to the Depression, moderate parties would likely have performed better in the 1930 and especially 1932 elections, and Nazism as a mass movement 'doesn't happen.'
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A striking counterfactual claim that a better monetary policy response, not just deeper ideological or historical forces, could have prevented the Nazi rise to power.
insights.quote: If the Brüning cabinet had a more effective monetary response to the economic crisis, you can imagine that the neither-Nazi-nor-Communist parties would have done a bit better in 1930 and way better in 1932 and Nazism doesn’t happen.
insights.locator: If the Brüning cabinet had a more effective

insights.claim: Yglesias argues Janet Yellen's decision to preemptively tighten monetary policy in 2016 while inflation remained below 2 percent was a mistake, and that slightly different Fed decision-making plausibly would have produced enough extra votes for Hillary Clinton to change the outcome of a very close election.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Extends the same monetary-policy-drives-elections logic to the 2016 U.S. election, implying Fed decisions may have been decisive in installing Trump.
insights.quote: it was a mistake of Janet Yellen to be preemptively tightening monetary conditions while inflation remained below 2 percent.
insights.locator: But the election was extremely close

insights.claim: Yglesias observes that tech executives and venture capitalists, despite their intelligence and business sophistication, tend to hold 'weird crank' opinions about macroeconomics relative to their competence in other domains.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A caution against treating tech-elite economic takes as automatically credible just because those same people are sharp on technology and business.
insights.quote: relative to their interests, intelligence, and basic worldview they tend to have weird crank opinions about macroeconomics.
insights.locator: My observation of tech executives and venture capitalists

insights.claim: Yglesias cites Blake Scholl's casual endorsement of the gold standard and Marc Andreessen's past insistence that GDP mismeasures the internet's economic impact via a 'wildly invalid methodology' as examples of Silicon Valley's crank macro views.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Names specific, prominent tech figures whose fringe macro claims have nonetheless circulated widely and shaped tech-world discourse.
insights.quote: Marc Andreessen used to insist that G.D.P. was mismeasuring the economic impact of the internet using a wildly invalid methodology.
insights.locator: You can see that in everything from Blake Scholl

insights.claim: Yglesias credits economist Tyler Cowen with having largely debunked the Andreessen-style 'GDP undercounts the internet' claim, noting it was widespread among tech figures 10-15 years ago and has since mostly vanished because tech readers follow Cowen's Marginal Revolution blog.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Illustrates how a single influential economist-blogger can shift consensus within an entire industry subculture over roughly a decade.
insights.quote: has now vanished because Tyler Cowen spent a lot of time specifically debunking it and tech guys (per Collison’s list) like to read Tyler Cowen.
insights.locator: That latter opinion was incredibly widespread

insights.claim: Yglesias recommends Milton Friedman's 'Money Mischief' as an accessible primer that could prevent tech elites from making basic macroeconomic mistakes, noting Cowen himself hasn't written much specifically on the gold-standard debate since around 2012.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A concrete, low-effort intervention suggestion for closing a specific knowledge gap among an influential group of decision-makers.
insights.quote: I might recommend Friedman’s “Money Mischief” as an accessible introduction to this basic topic that would prevent people from making dumb mistakes.
insights.locator: I might recommend Friedman’s

insights.claim: Yglesias argues that withdrawing from Afghanistan was the right strategic move for the United States and that the media's harsh treatment of Biden over the 2021 withdrawal was shameful and unfair.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Pushes back against a widely accepted media narrative that the withdrawal itself was Biden's defining failure.
insights.quote: Withdrawing from Afghanistan was the right strategic move for the United States.
insights.locator: While I have many criticisms of the Biden presidency

insights.claim: Over 20 years of the Afghanistan war there were 2,459 U.S. military deaths, nearly 2,000 civilian contractor deaths, more than a dozen CIA personnel deaths, and many allied-nation deaths, framing the 13 deaths during the 2021 withdrawal as low relative to the war's full human cost.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Puts the widely-cited 13 withdrawal deaths in the context of a 20-year toll roughly 300 times larger, challenging the proportionality of the media focus on the withdrawal alone.
insights.quote: over the course of 20 years of war there were 2,459 military deaths, plus nearly 2,000 civilian contractors, more than a dozen C.I.A. personnel, and many dead from various allied nations
insights.locator: But over the course of 20 years of war

insights.claim: Yglesias characterizes the media's focus on the withdrawal's execution rather than the 20-year policy failure that preceded it as 'shamefully successful media manipulation' that let the war's architects duck blame for their own conduct.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A pointed claim that political and media incentives, not the facts, determined which failure (the war itself vs. its final days) got blamed on whom.
insights.quote: The whole episode struck me as shamefully successful media manipulation by the architects of an egregious failure that was many years in the making
insights.locator: The whole episode struck me as shamefully successful

insights.claim: Yglesias proposes a more granular map of Democratic factions than a simple 'moderate vs. establishment' binary: a small but noisy leftist insurgent movement, a much larger and more influential 'progressive establishment' the insurgency sometimes targets and sometimes champions, a bloc of moderately moderate figures like the New Dem caucus, and a small but growing group of 'true moderates' like the House Blue Dogs.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Gives a sharper vocabulary for parsing intra-party fights, useful for anyone trying to predict which Democratic factions will actually clash over policy versus messaging.
insights.quote: There is a relatively small but very noisy real leftist insurgent movement afoot in the party right now.
insights.locator: Longer post on this coming

insights.claim: Yglesias describes the 'true moderate' faction he associates with as mounting a centrist critique of the Clinton/Biden/Harris/Schumer progressive establishment, explicitly not trying to defend that establishment's status quo.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Repositions self-identified moderates as reformers against the party's recent past rather than defenders of it, a distinction relevant to how they should campaign.
insights.quote: a centrist faction trying to mount a centrist critique of the Clinton / Biden / Harris / Schumer progressive establishment, not trying to defend that status quo.
insights.locator: This group is, as I’ve said before

insights.claim: Yglesias says he has pushed back on Third Way's leadership for front-loading anti-DSA messaging, arguing it turns moderates into 'dupes' for an establishment that doesn't listen to them on anything else.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Shows friction even within the moderate camp over strategy, warning that anti-left messaging can be co-opted by establishment actors for their own ends.
insights.quote: front-loading an anti-D.S.A. message turns moderates into dupes for an establishment that doesn’t listen to us about anything.
insights.locator: I’ve expressed to Third Way’s leaders

insights.claim: Yglesias cites Luke Bronin — an 'abundance guy' aligned with The Bench's moderate slate — defeating an incumbent House member who had the Working Families Party's endorsement as proof that anti-establishment politics doesn't require being a leftist.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A concrete electoral data point that moderates can successfully run as outsiders/challengers, undercutting the media habit of equating 'moderate' with 'establishment.'
insights.quote: he’s an abundance guy who is part of The Bench’s generally pretty moderate slate and he just knocked off an incumbent House member who scored the Working Families Party endorsement.
insights.locator: while I will not try to claim Luke Bronin

insights.claim: Yglesias's thesis is that fears upzoning would 'ruin' a beloved vacation destination like Cape Cod are overstated, because housing supply expansion self-limits once demand is satisfied, ultimately producing a new equilibrium with higher overall welfare than the constrained status quo.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Applies Yglesias's broader YIMBY framework to a harder case (charming, low-density vacation towns), arguing the same supply-and-demand logic still holds.
insights.quote: a new equilibrium eventually arises that has higher overall welfare and economic prosperity than under the old equilibrium.
insights.locator: Either way, a new equilibrium eventually arises

insights.claim: Barnstable County, Massachusetts (Cape Cod) has 581 people per square mile, compared with just 362 in Cumberland County — Maine's densest county and home to Portland — showing that a 'quaint' Massachusetts vacation area is already far denser than Maine's most urban county.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Undercuts the intuitive claim that Cape Cod is already 'full' or uniquely dense — it's less dense than it feels, and other regions considered rural are comparatively far emptier.
insights.quote: Barnstable County in Massachusetts has 581 people per square mile versus 362 in Cumberland County, which is Maine’s densest county and contains Portland and its suburbs.
insights.locator: When I looked up the numbers

insights.claim: Yglesias argues the ideal approach to vacation-town upzoning is to loosen zoning simultaneously across many towns at once (e.g., statewide in Maine) rather than in a single town, spreading disruption while maximizing the aggregate welfare gain.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A practical policy design point: concentrated single-town upzoning creates worse localized backlash than a coordinated regional approach.
insights.quote: In principle what you ought to do is upzone all the towns in Maine simultaneously.
insights.locator: Now obviously doing radical upzoning

insights.claim: Yglesias points to Miami Beach, Ocean City MD, and the dense French Riviera town of Juan-les-Pins as examples of highly dense vacation destinations that remain very popular, arguing increased density doesn't inherently 'ruin' a place — it just produces a different, still-desirable version of it.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Provides real-world counterexamples against the assumption that density and vacation-destination appeal are in tension.
insights.quote: Miami Beach is very popular. So is Ocean City, Md.
insights.locator: Similarly, if Cape Cod densified

themes.theme: Personal note on TMS for depression

insights.claim: Yglesias reports he tried transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) for depression after being annoyed by medication side effects, paid out of pocket since insurance typically only covers TMS for treatment-resistant depression, and felt it worked well despite acknowledging it's hard to properly placebo-test.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A candid personal data point on an alternative depression treatment that readers considering the same option might find directly useful.
insights.quote: I paid out of pocket and thought it worked great.
insights.locator: I was annoyed by some of the side effects of medication
